Hurricane Isaias has hit the U.S. Gulf Coast, leaving hundreds of thousands without power in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle. The storm made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida. It caused flooding and downed trees as it moved inland. Forecasters warn of life-threatening storm surges and possible tornadoes in the Southeast over the weekend.

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands without power after Isaias slams the Florida Panhandle and Alabama
articles.text:
Hundreds of thousands without power after Isaias slams the Florida Panhandle and Alabama | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
An American flag flaps in the wind generated by the effects of Isaias on an empty beach on Friday, Oct. 9, loom overhead on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, in Mon Louis Island, Ala. (AP Photo/Octavio Jones)
Isaias weakened overnight and was no longer considered a hurricane but flash flooding threats and the potential for tornadoes persisted Saturday as the storm moved inland across Alabama.
The storm, now considered a post-tropical cyclone, made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama as its wind speeds dropped sharply to 35 mph (55 kph). But the possibility of life-threatening storm surges still loomed for parts of the Florida Panhandle, along with a potential for 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) of rain across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend over the weekend.
Early Saturday, Isaias was about 25 miles (40 kilometers) south-southwest of Montgomery, Alabama and nearly 105 miles (170 kilometers) south of Birmingham, Alabama, with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph (55 kph), the NHC said Saturday. It is expected to move into the Tennessee Valley later Saturday and Sunday.
All tropical storm and storm surge warnings have been discontinued. But forecasters warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, as the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars, and seafood shacks.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference Friday.
Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
Strong hurricane winds blew the roof off a hotel in Pensacola and the city's mayor, D.C. Reeves, said on his Facebook page that the airport “took some damage.” Some power was out downtown, he said, and there were trees and power lines down in some areas.
Some Panhandle counties temporarily suspended emergency response Friday night because of dangerous conditions.
Parts of southern Alabama also were flooded, with officials in Mobile reporting downed trees and power lines. Roads in Houston County, which is in the southeastern corner of the state, were closed because of similar conditions.
More than 915,000 customers in Florida, Alabama and Georgia were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
Tim Mowry, who rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, said the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack in his patio door. He lost power around 4:30 p.m. but was able to rely on a generator. Standing water also covered his backyard, and parts of his fence were ripped down, but overall he said the storm wasn’t as bad as he expected.
“As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate,” Mowry said.
Mowry said his son, who lives about 15 minutes away, tried to drive to his home after losing power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the roads.
Isaias, the first hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, is also expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.
The storm also grounded most Friday flights at several panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened into a Category 4 hurricane as it approached Mexico’s coast.
Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

articles.title: Education group will try again after ads criticizing Boston schools pulled by MBTA
articles.text:
Education group will try again after ads criticizing Boston schools pulled by MBTA | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
An education advocacy group behind a provocative new ad campaign skewering Boston Public Schools for “failing” some elementary students is trying again after its original ads were pulled last week by the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority after barely a day.
The initial ads displayed a close-up photo of a child’s eyes, stamped with a slogan blaring, “BPS is Failing Her.” (Other versions use images of a different child and the pronouns “him” and “them.”)
Underneath ran a tagline stating, “70% of third graders can’t read or do math at grade level,” along with the phrase, “We can fix it, together.”
A version of the original ad about BPS reading and math levels that appeared on the T before it was pulled. (Courtesy of Next Chapter Boston)
About 150 ads were installed on subway cars on the Red, Orange, and Green Lines, two commuter rail lines and bus stops in preparation for the campaign’s launch Monday, said Mary Tamer, a local education advocate spearheading the project. But the ads were yanked within 24 hours after some ads were put up ahead of schedule on the Red Line and spotted by the Boston Globe, which reached out to city officials.
“ I understand that this is a really hard truth and that they clearly don't want it out there, which is why they squashed these MBTA ads,” Tamer said.
The city of Boston says it had nothing to do with the ads' removal. But officials do take umbrage with the message.
A Boston city spokesperson said in a statement, “neither the city nor BPS has had any communications with the MBTA regarding its decision to either place or remove these ads.”
The statement added that "Spending millions of dollars on a political ad campaign that uses images of children and misleading rhetoric" is "both cynical and deeply unproductive."
A statement from Boston Public Schools acknowledged that the district was aware of the advertisements without going into further detail.
“Our focus remains on improving the education for all of our students and ensuring each student is prepared for success beyond the classroom,” the BPS statement said.
The signs are part of an extensive $1.5 million ad campaign through an initiative called Next Chapter Boston, led by Tamer and Vernée Wilkinson.
Tamer is a former BPS parent, former Boston school committee member and founder of the education advocacy group MassPotential. She previously had been vocal about preserving the MCAS high school graduation requirement before it was repealed by voters in a 2024 ballot initiative.
She said the goal of the campaign is to draw attention to data around math and reading rates in BPS and spur the public to get involved.
“The frustration for so many of us has reached a peak and we knew that we had to do something bold in a desperate attempt to get BPS to do the right thing,” Tamer said in an interview. She said she wants the district to use “evidence-based practices and high quality instructional materials” and to more closely analyze data to create accountability metrics.
Wilkinson is a parent who describes herself as a "longtime Boston community advocate."
"We find that the majority of Boston residents and folks in the surrounding area aren't attentive or aware of the fact of the state of Boston Public Schools and that students are challenged," she said.
In the spring 2026 MCAS standardized test results, state data shows 31% of third graders in Boston met or exceeded proficiency in reading, compared with 43% of students statewide. In math, 30% of Boston students met proficiency, compared to 42% statewide. A district statement said students in grades 3 to 8 "demonstrated typical growth, or academic progress, as compared to their peers across the state."
The ad campaign was also deployed on streaming platforms, including Hulu and YouTube, and on large billboards along I-93 in the both north and south directions.
In a statement, the MBTA said the ads "did not comply with the viewpoint neutral restrictions contained in the MBTA guidelines relating to standards and permissible categories for advertising on MBTA property" and didn't undergo required review.
An email obtained by WBUR between a T contractor and a Next Chapter Boston vendor reveals the ads were pulled for allegedly violating MBTA advertising guidelines, specifically ads it considers “demeaning or disparaging,”“false, misleading or deceptive” and those dealing with libel or intellectual property infringement.
Wilkinson contends the fact the ads were initially posted then immediately taken down by the MBTA is a form of censorship.
“There hasn't been a great deal of clarity around why the ads were removed, so it's our best understanding that there's somebody that has enough power and leverage to remove this messaging,” she said.
Nonetheless, she said Next Chapter Boston is working to amend the ad campaign.
“We’ve submitted some alternative language and we’re waiting to hear back if that has been approved or not,” Tamer said, adding that at least one new proposed slogan, “She Deserves Better” was also rejected by the transit authority. Meantime, the group is considering other ways it can promote its message.
Asked about the funding behind Next Chapter Boston, Tamer said the “absolute bulk of the money is coming from Boston donors" plus contributions from an out of state foundation she declined to name but said "funds mission-driven organizations."
She said the most significant contributions come from Rick Burnes, co-founder of the venture capital firm Charles River Ventures, and Michael Champa, a Boston resident and former Stoughton public high school teacher. She declined to name other donors.
In an interview, Champa described the initiative's supporters as "a group of people who have been involved in watching Boston Public Schools for decades who believe we can do better. We have no other motivation other than that, plain

articles.title: Question 8: Mass. voters weigh measure that would topple recreational marijuana industry
articles.text:
Question 8: Mass. voters weigh measure that would topple recreational marijuana industry | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
A prepackaged container of cannabis from the Massachusetts-based company Root & Bloom being sold at SEED dispensary in Somerville. (Jesse Costa/WBUR)
Ten years ago, Massachusetts voters legalized the sale of recreational cannabis. On Nov. 3, they'll get another chance at the ballot box to either re-declare their support, or reverse course and upend the state’s sprawling weed industry.
Over the decade since the 2016 ballot measure ushered in the legal adult-use marijuana market, Massachusetts has become home to some 400 dispensaries and another 200 businesses dedicated to growing, transporting and supporting cannabis sales. And retailers have brought in an estimated $330 million in local and state tax revenue.
If passed, this year’s ballot question would collapse the $8 billion industry, while leaving intact rules that allow for the sales of medical marijuana and the limited possession of pot for recreational use. It would make Massachusetts the first state to repeal recreational cannabis.
What would Question 8 do?
Question 8 will ask voters whether to repeal the laws that made Massachusetts the sixth state in the country to legalize recreational marijuana sales.
Possession of up to one ounce, and five grams of concentrated products, would remain legal for people over 21, as would home cultivation. (Current law allows residents of age to carry up to two ounces and grow six plants for personal use.)
Recreational dispensaries would be able to apply on an expedited basis for medical licenses.
The new law would go into effect in 2028.
A “yes” vote is one in favor of repeal. A “no” vote would keep the status quo.
What do supporters argue?
Question 8 is backed by the Coalition for a Healthy Massachusetts, a ballot initiative group mostly funded by a single source: Smart Approaches to Marijuana Action Inc. The Virginia-based group has contributed nearly $3.5 million to the repeal effort.
Kevin Sabet, who heads the nonprofit, served as a drug policy advisor under the administrations of former Presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama.
The cannabis industry is leading the country “right into the mess that Big Tobacco created for over a century of lying to the American people about the harms of cigarettes,” Sabet said. “The marijuana industry is just taking that same playbook and applying it to high-potency THC.”
Sabet pointed to research that links legalization to an increase in mental health problems among adolescents in Massachusetts, as well as increased cannabis exposure cases among young children.
A post-legalization study out of Mass General Brigham suggested that recreational cannabis sales “may disproportionately affect” adolescents with psychiatric issues. Researchers found a nearly fourfold increase in cannabis-related disorders among adolescents receiving emergency psychiatric care. Researchers found no significant change in disorder rates among adults.
Sabet said the industry is profiting from addiction.
“This wasn't a moral crusade,” Sabet said. “The idea that we would be rolling out the red carpet for an industry encouraging a sort of addiction-for-profit-style industry, to me, was just something that I thought was really not good.”
Question 8 title on the mail-in ballot for the 2026 Massachusetts state election. (Jesse Costa/WBUR)
Sabet said the ballot effort is about “forcing the conversation” around the harm of marijuana, even if the campaign faces an uphill battle.
“We're under no illusions that the bluest state in the country is going to pass this easily with flying colors,” he said. “But we want to have that conversation.”
Sabet said the “yes” campaign does not seek to disrupt the medical use market, which he said should be up to health officials and not voters.
“Question 8 is simply about the commercialization of marijuana,” he said. “It doesn't touch the individual's right to use.”
It would, however, affect a person’s ability to purchase legal marijuana in Massachusetts.
What do opponents argue?
Registered in opposition to the repeal is the Committee to Protect Cannabis Regulation. The group has raised $2.3 million from a host of contributors, including donations of $100,000 or more from three industry groups and the Retailers Association of Massachusetts.
Ryan Dominguez is head of  the Massachusetts Cannabis Coalition, a trade group opposing the repeal. He said that ending the sale of cannabis will force users back to the illicit market.
“ Without a regulated system, they're going to have to buy products that are not tested, not age-gated, and may be laced with other things,” Dominguez said. “You're inviting in folks like the cartels to come in and have a new business.”
Massachusetts Cannabis Coalition Executive Director Ryan Dominguez speaks with Garth Goldstein about why he should vote "no" on Question 8 outside the SEED dispensary in Somerville. (Jesse Costa/WBUR)
Instead of driving down demand, Dominguez said prohibition would send users out of state to buy cannabis, siphoning tax revenue out of Massachusetts and toppling an industry that he said employs more than 20,000 people.
Asked about the adverse effects of marijuana use among minors, Dominguez pointed to data that suggests declining consumption rates.
Centers for Disease Control data indicates that use among high school students in Massachusetts has gone down significantly since legalization. In 2019, 26% of students reported using cannabis during the previous 30 days — in 2025, just 12% reported use, mirroring a national decline.
Use among adults, meanwhile, seems to have gone up. Statewide numbers from 2023 indicate that 18.2% of adults surveyed said they’d used cannabis in the past year, compared to 12.9% in 2018. (The state’s first recreational dispensaries opened in November of that year.)

articles.title: Affordable ‘passive’ homes replace longtime vacant lots in Dorchester
articles.text:
Affordable ‘passive’ homes replace longtime vacant lots in Dorchester | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
The three new houses on Norwell Street. (Courtesy of Jane Messinger/DOT Design Collaborative)
Two Dorchester real estate professionals have joined forces to launch a new development company focused on their own neighborhood — and their first project, a 12-unit, three-building complex on Norwell Street, is now nearing full occupancy.
Jennifer Ha, an architect and co-founder of Hue Architecture, and Milo Stella, who operates Star Contracting, formed DOT Design Collaborative in 2023. Their first development together is at 104-108 Norwell St., where three new buildings — each with four condo units — have been constructed over the last year on what were once city-owned vacant lots.
As of this week, one unit— a three-bedroom priced at $393,120— is still on the market through the City of Boston’s Housing Office and their Welcome Home, Boston initiative. The units are offered via lottery to qualified applicants.
Milo Stella, left, and Jennifer Ha hold up a rendering of their passive houses. (Seth Daniel/Dorchester Reporter)
For Ha and Stella, the project is a “proof of concept” to show how affordable housing in Boston can include innovative building techniques, durable materials, energy efficiency, and higher-end architectural details.
Ha and Stella had previously been approached separately to work on other affordable housing developments, including projects associated with the first phase of Welcome Home, Boston. When neither was selected for a bid in the first round, they decided to combine forces.
“We knew we could do an outstanding job for our neighborhood,” Ha said. “Why does this have to be a lost opportunity when we can actually come together and build what we believe can be what’s right for our neighborhood?”
The resulting company, DOT Design Collaborative, was formed ahead of its successful bid for the Norwell Street property in the Four Corners neighborhood. The 12 deed-restricted condos range from studios to three-bedroom units and are reserved for income-qualified buyers. Half of the homes are available to households at 80% of area median income and half at 100% AMI, Stella said.
A kitchen inside one of the units at 104 Norwell St. in Dorchester. (Courtesy of Jane Messinger/DOT Design Collaborative)
What separates the project from many similar small-scale developments, Ha and Stella say, is its construction standard. All three buildings are being certified under the Passive House standard, an energy-efficient building approach that emphasizes a tight building envelope, insulation, ventilation, comfort, indoor air quality, and sharply reduced energy consumption.
The buildings include rooftop solar panels that will be owned by the future condo associations. The combination of solar power and lower energy consumption should help residents control utility and condominium costs over the long term.
The developers also used a prefabricated construction system supplied by Bensonwood, a New Hampshire manufacturer. Exterior walls, floors, and roof systems were largely fabricated indoors before being transported to Dorchester and assembled by crane. Windows, insulation, and weather barriers were already incorporated into the panels.
Once the foundations were complete, Stella said, work crews were able to assemble and weatherproof each of the buildings in roughly three weeks. That method did not necessarily save money upfront, he said, but reduced exposure to weather delays and allowed more of the construction to take place under controlled factory conditions.
“We knew it was going to be more expensive than the typical build,” he added. “We did not want to meet the minimum standard. We wanted to go beyond.”
A view of the site on Norwell Street in 2023 before construction started through the City of Boston’s Welcome Home, Boston initiative. (Seth Daniel/Dorchester Reporter)
Construction costs are roughly $6 million, according to Ha and Stella, with total development costs of about $7.9 million. The project relied on city subsidy funds, matching assistance from MassHousing, and financing through a “mission-driven lender.”
“What we were able to accomplish on our project was really only possible because of the subsidy structure that we were able to tap into,” Stella said.
“I think it’s an argument for why these subsidies are critical and why we need to continue to fund those grant programs,” he said. “We can’t fix the macro-economic situation of land costs and construction costs in the city of Boston. But, if we have the resources available to us, we can accomplish great things.”
The Norwell Street units went into the market through the city’s website in May, and by early October nearly all but one had been reserved. Two homeowners moved in on Sept. 18, with several more closings expected this month and full occupancy anticipated by mid-November.
“The Norwell Street development shows exactly what the Wu administration is working to accomplish through Welcome Home, Boston by creating more opportunities for Boston residents to own a home and build a future in the neighborhoods they love,” said Sheila Dillon, Boston’s chief of Housing.
“These new homes are well designed, energy-efficient, close to transit, and, most importantly, priced so that income-qualified homebuyers have a real opportunity to purchase them. Homeownership is an important way families can create stability, and we’re proud to help create that opportunity here in Dorchester.”
The final available unit — a three bedroom, first-floor unit — is still open for buyers. Contact Syliva Adorno, senior program manager at the Boston Home Center, for more details.
“I do hope that we can have more projects like this,” Ha said. “I am very proud that we have accomplished this and that we can show through the neighborhood we can do better.”

articles.title: How a local costume shop is competing with Spirit Halloween and Amazon this spooky season
articles.text:
How a local costume shop is competing with Spirit Halloween and Amazon this spooky season | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Costumes and decades clothing at the Garment District. (Courtesy Eric Propp)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's Saturday morning newsletter, The Weekender. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox,  sign up here.
Halloween is officially three weeks away, but for Cambridge-based Boston Costume, the busy season isn’t just about the spookiest night of the year.
“When school starts back up, that’s when everyone kind of says, ‘OK, summer’s over. Time to get back to work.’ And then out of that, events start popping up,” Eric Propp, rental supervisor at Boston Costume, said. “It doesn’t even have to be Halloween-related.”
September usually brings renaissance fairs, themed weddings and Oktoberfest celebrations, Propp said. And this year, the company is coming off a buzzier-than-usual summer with America’s 250th, after renting out colonial costumes to Massachusetts cities, towns and pro athletes. (Yes, they were the ones behind the Bruins’ stylish arrival in Tampa back in February, according to Propp.)
Still, being a year-round costume store can be “tricky,” Propp added. And around Halloween, people have options — they can thrift their costumes, pull from their closets, or buy from retailers like Spirit Halloween and Amazon. Propp and I talked about how Boston Costume has pivoted in recent years to keep up.
Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Hanna Ali: How does the store prepare for Halloween each year?
Eric Propp:  “Many years ago, we would do a lot of package costumes, so then it was definitely trying to pick up on trends or anticipate what would be big. And even then, it was always tough because I feel like every year there's something that happens mid-October kind of culturally … then all of a sudden everyone wants to be that thing.  So then the industry —as much as it tries — it can't adapt quick enough. Maybe there's some place in China, some cosplay website that can bang out something quick, but most everyone will miss that last-minute, hot item.
“ We [now] try to corner a different market, carrying more accessories and things for more DIY. We have a DIY costume section, and we really rely on the Garment District, which is just right in the same building on the second floor. So, people can kind of put together a lot of different things without us even trying to guess what's gonna be hot.”
HA: What's it been like having to compete with Spirit Halloween popping all up over the place?
EP: “ For years, we were always competing with them, and then even other places. And that again is another reason where we've just decided to pivot and just be a different type of place with a different flavor. If they pop up somewhere kind of close, it's not that we don't pay attention to it, but we don't have to worry.”
HA: Is there a particular local edge you're able to provide that a big-box retailers can't?
EP: “That's where the rental department really shines. People at the last minute come in and say, ‘Oh, my Amazon's not gonna arrive in time. Here I am.’ They paid them, it didn't work; or they bought something and it was flimsy and they hated it. We do have pop culture items. We have ‘Star Wars.’ But we'll have a Darth Vader that's got more armor pieces. Stormtroopers that are deluxe. Iron Man and Master Chief. Things like that where the quality is much better.
“If they were to have to go buy these items, a whole package would be more like $1,000. Whereas for us you spend $100, $110, maybe $125, and you can get head to toe covered in a look that's specific and unique.  And then, you return it. You don't have to worry about what you're gonna do with it.
“[We’re also a ] two-in-one store. You can find a real vintage piece, a real '60s or '70s dress, get a wig, get stage makeup or get a rental. If you don't know what to do for Halloween, just walk in with an open mind, and find that unique piece that really kind of pops to you, and then build something around it.”
Orc costumes by Eric Propp. (Courtesy Eric Propp)
HA: What’s your favorite among those elaborate rental costumes?
EP: “I had made these three giant Orc monster costumes for a play for Northeastern about five or six years ago, and luckily I was able to bring them with me and put them into rentals over here, so they're just kind of these very deluxe funny items. They have big, crazy armor and muscles.”
HA: Do you have any predictions for what might be the most popular Halloween costumes this year?
EP: “A lot of people are going colonial, so I think the 250th is still kind of hitting a little bit for Halloween.  We're definitely getting a lot of requests for couples doing kind of colonial Revolutionary War era. And then as far as pop culture things, ‘The Odyssey’ and ‘Spider-Man’ were big movies. ‘Obsession,’ potentially — horror movies can always do well, and if you kind of look like the characters then you can pull it off for really cheap.”
HA: What are some costumes that have wowed you in the past?
EP: “[Last year] when the East Wing got demolished, I was like, ‘OK, who's showing up as the half-demolished White House?’ And sure enough someone made this giant architectural piece with bulldozers, so I thought that was clever. I am definitely waiting for people to be the reflecting pool … or the phantom of the Kennedy Center.”
P.S. — This Halloween, we want to see some Boston-themed costumes! If you, a friend, family member or pet have previously used our great city as inspiration for a Halloween costume, submit your photos here Oct. 20 and they could be included in a round up later this month.

articles.title: Prisoner death at MCI-Norfolk raises questions about suicide prevention efforts
articles.text:
Prisoner death at MCI-Norfolk raises questions about suicide prevention efforts | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
The apparent suicide of a prisoner at MCI-Norfolk this week is raising questions about the suicide prevention and mental health reforms underway at Massachusetts prisons.
The Department of Correction is promising a thorough review of what led to the death of 29-year-old Emil Encarnacion. He was being held in what's known as a behavior assessment unit, where prisoners are held if they might pose a risk to themselves or others. Those units came under scrutiny earlier this year after an independent report commissioned by the department showed that three of the six suicides in state prisons in 2025 were in such units.
According to the department, correction officers responded a report of self-harm in the behavior assessment unit at MCI-Norfolk Monday. Encarnacion died a short time later at a local hospital.
"We extend our sincere sympathies to Mr. Encarnacion's family, loved ones and all those impacted by his passing," the Department of Correction statement said.
The department said it is working on several improvements recommended in the independent report that it commissioned after six suicides in state prisons last year. Those improvements include more staff training, improved access to mental health care and the creation of an overnight helpline for prisoners to reach out.

articles.title: Boston Public Schools is on the market for bus-mounted cameras to catch stop-sign runners
articles.text:
Boston Public Schools is on the market for bus-mounted cameras to catch stop-sign runners | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Jesse Costa/WBUR
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's daily morning newsletter, WBUR Today. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here.
There was a late update Thursday evening in the killing of a Reading woman inside her home. Police in Vermont spotted and arrested the victim's son, Ryan Hanafin, 22, hours after Reading cops and Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan called him a person of interest in his mother's shooting. The family's younger son was home at the time of the killing, according to Ryan, but their daughter was away at college.
This is the second time in two months the Middlesex DA stood before reporters to allege someone in her county committed matricide. Back in August, an Acton teen was charged with killing his mother and younger brother. Investigators in that case said Arjun Aravind, 17, had been writing online fiction, including themes of family murder, in the months leading up to his arrest.
Now, to the rest of the news:
Boston just put the word out: The city's school district is in the market for bus-mounted cameras to catch stop-sign runners. The city and school department on Thursday said they plan to add so-called stop-arm cameras to the city's bus fleet, and asked for bids from companies that do this sort of work. The bid said the district will start with 25 buses to gather data before rolling out more cams.
How it works: When a school bus rolls to a stop and the driver activates the little stop sign arm near the front of the vehicle, the camera turns on. If a driver blows by the bus, the camera will grab images of scofflaw's car and license plate.
Positive results elsewhere: Boston's not the first Massachusetts community to try bus cams. Peabody set up a pilot program in September 2023, adding cameras to 10 school buses. More than 3,400 drivers were photographed running the bus-mounted stop sign, according to a CBS Boston report. Over in Salem, a three-month pilot program nabbed pics of 3,000-plus bus runners.
What they're saying: Speaking with WBUR's Suevon Lee, City Councilor Enrique Pepén called the program a "huge step forward" for kids and parents. " This is the first time that we are getting so close to doing some type of — any type of — enforcement, honestly, or to hold drivers accountable if they run the stop sign on school buses."
Big Brother on the bus?: Pepén was quick to note these cameras aren't like Flock or other always-on surveillance tools that have people worried. Instead, these cameras only turn on when the bus' little flashing stop sign swings out and uses artificial intelligence to detect when the car rolls past the stop sign. License plate images would also only be stored for 14 days.
Jury selection in the time of TikTok: Opening statements are expected to begin today in the murder trial of former Stoughton police officer Matthew Farwell, who is accused of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child. It follows what was a tricky jury selection process this week, according to WBUR's Patrick Madden. That's because just like recent high-profile trials involving Karen Read and Lindsay Clancy, this case is also gaining a pretty big social media following.
One key question prospective jurors faced: How much they've learned about the case, through more traditional media like a newspaper or local radio, or through social media platforms like YouTube or TikTok. "The proliferation of information on social media makes it harder to get an impartial jury," former prosecutor Glenn MacKinlay, of lawfirm McCarter and English, told Patrick.
Zoom in: One prospective juror was removed from the pool after saying she followed the Karen Read case closely on YouTube and Instagram. She also mentioned having opinions on the police officers and department involved in this case.
PSA to ferry fans: You can now track the MBTA's ferry boats in real time. The agency launched the new feature on its MBTA Go app this week. That means T riders can now follow all modes of transit from a smart phone, not just those landlocked lines.
Plus a good night for sports fans: The Bruins had a 6-1 win over the Utah Mammoth last night at TD Garden, with big thanks to captain David Pastrnak leading the team with 2 goals and 2 assists. And the Celtics won their preseason opener against the Cavaliers in Cleveland, 124-113. They'll both be back on their respective home ice and court tomorrow and, coincidentally, they're both taking on teams from the land of cheesesteaks, Philadelphia.
P.S.— Franklin Park is set to get a new monument. What is it dedicated to? Take our Boston News Quiz to test your knowledge of this week's biggest news moments.
